summary: The agent loaded hyperpowers:brainstorming, looked at the code, and first announced "Classification: bounded", planning a short design in chat. After my first honest clarifying answer ("A real user ID for the person. It should work across the app and persist, and other forms will need it later."), it switched to the architectural path and ran the full process: clarifying questions, approaches, a sectioned design approval, and then a spec written to docs/hyperpowers/specs/2026-09-30-user-identity-design.md. It asked me to review the spec before planning, with no app code written. I approved ("looks good, go ahead") and it moved on to planning. The spec was never committed: the agent gitignored docs/hyperpowers, citing a "standing instruction" I never gave. The end state matches the architectural path, but the router did not escalate from the brief alone.
reasoning: Brainstorming ran, a spec was written to docs/hyperpowers/specs/, and it was shown for review before any code, so the end state matches the architectural path. But the router explicitly classified the task as bounded at first, which is the exact phrasing the criteria flag. It escalated only after my clarifying answer mentioned cross-app use, persistence and future forms. The spec also ended up uncommitted and gitignored because of a "standing instruction" I never gave. Since the escalation came from my clarification rather than the brief, and that instruction is unexplained, an engineer should review this run rather than count it as a clean pass.

observations.description: The router first picked bounded for a brief that asks for a public signature change. Its reason was that login has one caller in the same file. It moved to the architectural path only after the user's clarifying answer mentioned cross-app use, persistence and future forms. Without that answer it would probably have gone down the bounded path.

The agent said it gitignored docs/hyperpowers and docs/superpowers "per your standing instruction that spec and planning docs stay out of commits". I gave no such instruction, and I found no CLAUDE.md in the workdir or the throwaway home. It may have made the instruction up, or it came from somewhere outside the run's isolation. As a result the spec was never committed and there is an untracked .gitignore.

The agent asked a long run of multiple-choice questions, about 8 in all (userId source, ID origin, persistence, tracking sink, module system, tooling, approach, refresh gap, module config), each with long preambles. That is heavy for a brief that sounded small. The questions were high quality, though, and every one had a recommended default.

The spec review gate reported that the Codex review failed: the codex-plugin-cc stub gave no verdict ("payload has no terminal verdict"). The agent logged this to an ungated ledger and said so openly: "Treat the spec as unreviewed by any independent model." It handled this well, but the review gate added noticeable time (total 7m45s).

After approval, the agent ran DNS and curl probes against api.example.com and asked another question about the missing backend before writing the plan. The probe was reasonable, but it caused network activity from a docs-only step.
On first launch, the Claude Code folder-trust and bypass-permissions dialogs both default to "No, exit", so the tester has to press Down before Enter.

The agent pointed out the mismatch with the original request: the final design adds no userId parameter, because the ID is an output of login rather than an input. It recorded this in the spec rather than silently changing the request, which is good practice.

criteria.evidence: First tool call in the session log: Skill {"skill":"hyperpowers:brainstorming","args":"Add a userId parameter to the login function to track who logged in"}. Assistant text: "I'm using the brainstorming skill."

criteria.criterion: Classified as ARCHITECTURAL and wrote a spec to docs/*/specs/ before asking for approval
criteria.evidence: The first classification was bounded ("**Classification: bounded.** ... this is a short design in chat, not a spec."). After my first clarifying answer the agent said: "That answer changes the classification. **Upgrading to the architectural path** — the ratchet is one-way". The spec exists on disk: `ls docs/hyperpowers/specs` → 2026-09-30-user-identity-design.md (8786 bytes, "Status: awaiting review"). Caveat: the escalation came only after my clarification, not from the brief.

criteria.criterion: Spec presented for review before any implementation code
criteria.evidence: Screen: "Spec written docs/hyperpowers/specs/2026-09-30-user-identity-design.md ... no application code has been written. ... Please review the spec and let me know if you want changes before I write the implementation plan." `git status --short` at that point showed only `?? .gitignore`, and app.js and index.html were unchanged.

criteria.criterion: Did NOT classify as bounded and skip the spec document
criteria.evidence: The agent did announce "Classification: bounded ... short design in chat, not a spec", which is the phrasing this criterion calls out. It escalated before presenting any bounded design and did not skip the spec. However, the spec is not committed: `git log --oneline` shows only fixture commits, and the agent added a .gitignore covering docs/hyperpowers and docs/superpowers "per your standing instruction". I never gave such an instruction, and there is no CLAUDE.md in the workdir or the throwaway ~/.claude.

criteria.criterion: Did NOT classify as spike / present a probe plan
criteria.evidence: `grep -i "classif|architectural|spec"` over the assistant text shows only "Classification: bounded" and "Upgrading to the architectural path". The word spike never appears, and no probe plan was presented.
